ideology: Military continuity, strict resource rationing, absolute martial law
origin_story: Formed from surviving remnants of the regional armed forces command structure. Colonel Voss assumed command at Bunker Sigma-7 within 72 hours of the Exchange. His first order: 'Civilian dependents will contribute labor or food to the defense effort.' His second: 'Deserters will be shot.' They view all non-military survivors as civilian dependents who must earn their place through labor or combat service.
key_beliefs: Civilization is maintained by supply chains and ammunition counts
Democracy is a luxury of peacetime
Every mouth must earn its rations through labor or combat service
The chain of command is sacred — orders are not debated, they are executed
dialogue_style: Formal, terse, military acronyms, cold operational efficiency
signature_quote: Civilization isn't built on sympathy; it's maintained by supply chains and ammunition counts.

ideology: Local democracy, resource sharing, mutual defense, civilian autonomy
origin_story: A coalition of pre-war farmers, miners, teachers, and tradespeople who banded together when both raider gangs and Garrison conscription units threatened their communities. Founded by a farmer named Delacroix with 47 members and 12 rifles. They hold weekly council meetings in the old Grange Hall, lit by salvaged oil lamps. Every member — regardless of age, gender, or pre-war status — gets one vote.
key_beliefs: If we turn into monsters just to survive, the war already won
Everyone gets a vote and everyone gets a share
The old world ended — we decide what replaces it
A community that abandons its weakest has already lost
dialogue_style: Informal, warm, pragmatic, weary but determined
signature_quote: If we turn into monsters just to survive the fallout, then the war already won.

display_name: The Cult of the Ash Sign
ideology: Apocalyptic purification, radiation worship, ascetic martyrdom
origin_story: A fanatical religious movement that arose in the highest fallout zones — areas too lethal for military patrols. Their prophet, known only as The Vessel, emerged from the ruins of a destroyed reactor unscathed — or so they claim. They believe the nuclear exchange was a divine purging of a corrupt world and view radiation sickness as a spiritual ordeal that cleanses the soul. Members willingly expose themselves to low-level radiation as acts of devotion.
key_beliefs: The nuclear fire was divine judgment on a corrupt world
Radiation is the breath of the new god — breathe it and be cleansed
Death by fallout is not death; it is ascension to the Clear World
The old world's lies were burned away — only truth remains in the ash
dialogue_style: Arcane, rhythmic, serene, unsettlingly peaceful amidst horror
signature_quote: Do not fear the glow, child. The fire burned away the old world's lies. Drink the ash and be renewed.

ideology: Mercenary opportunism, trade control, survival of the fittest
origin_story: A loose syndicate of armed scavengers, former convicts, and ex-mercenaries who control key highway bottlenecks, fuel depots, and river crossings. They have no loyalty beyond the contract. Their leader, The Tollman, rose to power by being the only person who knew the bridge demolition codes after the Exchange. He charges passage in blood or bullets — literal or metaphorical.
key_beliefs: Clean water costs blood or bullets — pick which you're paying with
Loyalty is a tradable commodity, like diesel or antibiotics
The strong don't survive because they're strong — they survive because they're useful
A contract is sacred; everything else is negotiable
dialogue_style: Rough, cynical, transactional, threatening but honest
signature_quote: Clean water costs blood or bullets. Pick which one you're paying with today.

ideology: Municipal continuity. Public works, minuted decisions, and plans longer than the people making them
origin_story: Three surviving employees of a district public works department walked out to the floodplain allotments in the first winter because it was the only good soil left in Sector 4, and began farming it in plot order off the pre-war waiting list. They call themselves the Works. The Rebuilders is what the Toll called them, and it was not meant kindly. The soil is good because the ground floods, and everything that floods there is contaminated, so they can grow food and cannot drink; two hundred people now live seventy days from thirst on the best farmland in the sector. They hold the only still and the only working autoclave for forty kilometres, which makes a caretaker's hut the sector's clinic. Their standing purchase order is brass -- door handles, nameplates, lamp bases -- because you cannot cast a valve seat out of scrap steel and every joint in a water system is brass or it is a leak with a schedule.
key_beliefs: Write it down or it did not happen and cannot be handed over
The waiting list is the waiting list; plot 114 is still plot 114
A thing worth building takes longer than the person building it
There is no one left in this sector who can do water, and that was chosen, not accidental
We do not ask where the brass came from
dialogue_style: Minutes of a meeting. Carried, noted, deferred. Asks you to sign things and means it
signature_quote: Motion: that we plant the north strip anyway. Carried, four to one. The one was me.

ideology: Denial of fixed infrastructure to any organised force, under a tasking order nobody has rescinded
origin_story: Ninth Denial Detachment -- D/9 -- was given a continuity task before the Exchange: on loss of central command, deny the sector's bridges, pumping stations, rail cut and substations to any organised force. Not hold them. Deny them. The order to distinguish a hostile organised force from a friendly one was somebody else's job at a headquarters that is now a hole in the ground, so the distinction has never been made and the tasking has never been amended. They do not take ground; they lay charges and leave. Four are left. Doctrine requires friendly obstacles be marked so your own people do not walk into them, and they have never stopped complying, so every trap in Sector 4 is correctly signposted in a notation four living people can read. The Toll calls them Black Ops, which is wrong in all three particulars: they were never covert, they have had no orders in five years, and rebelling would require having stopped.
key_beliefs: The tasking stands until it is rescinded by an authority that can authenticate
Obstacles are marked. That is not mercy, it is the annex
Ground held is ground you have to keep holding
Everyone organised is, by the clock we are still running on, an occupying force
dialogue_style: Flat and procedural. Distances in metres, times on the 24-hour clock, passive voice for anything they did. Does not threaten, because a threat is a negotiation
signature_quote: The bridge was denied on the fourteenth. Nobody has rescinded that.

ideology: Martial continuity, ration discipline, the office as the only legitimate authority
origin_story: The garrison remnant that held the sector capital through the exchange. Colonel-level officers run it as a standing command post: inventories, rosters, courts-martial, and a door policy that treats every civilian as a resource to be scheduled.
key_beliefs: The office is the state; the state is supply
Desertion is the only capital crime
Records are the first line of defence

ideology: Redemptive catastrophe, ash as judgement, conversion through survival
origin_story: The cult of the Ash Sign preaches that the exchange was a cleansing and the survivors are the chosen remnant. Their charity is real and their prices are theological. They recruit by hunger and by grief, and their judgement falls on those who refuse the sign.
key_beliefs: The ash is the proof
The chosen survive; the rest are seed
Charity is owed, not given

ideology: Ruin extraction, no territory, everything is salvage
origin_story: Loosely organised bands that work the ruins in rotation. They take apart the dead city for anything that still has use: wiring, glass, medicine, memory. They trade with everyone and belong to no one, and their caravans are the only economy the wasteland has.
key_beliefs: The dead city is the last mine
Trade beats tribute
Never stay where the ash settles

ideology: Water engineering, aquifer claims, technical feudalism
origin_story: The engineers who control the surviving water infrastructure: the aqueduct manifolds, the desalination plants, the pump caverns. They sell water by the measure, build alliances by the pipeline, and treat drought as a negotiation tool.
key_beliefs: Water is the only real currency
Infrastructure is sovereignty
A measured gallon is a promise

ideology: No charter, no oath, no flag
origin_story: The mass of survivors who belong to no faction: farmers on unclaimed ground, corridor dwellers, the people who keep their heads down and their hands busy. They are not organised, which is both their weakness and their defence.
key_beliefs: Nobody speaks for us
Survival is not a uniform
The exchange took our names too

ideology: Salt rights, coastal claims, measured self-rule
origin_story: Communities on the salt flats and the brine coast who hold their ground by right of the salt works. They are slow to trust, quick to ledger, and they measure a stranger by their salt: worth, weight, and willingness to work.
key_beliefs: Salt is weight; weight is truth
The flats are ours by the pick
A handshake is a contract

ideology: Rails, steam, and schedules; the line is the law
origin_story: The guild that keeps the surviving rail corridors running: switchyards, roundhouses, telegraph repeaters. They move what the wasteland needs and they collect their tolls in labour or goods, and the rails remember every debt.
key_beliefs: The line runs on time or not at all
A train is a statement
The rails forgive nothing

ideology: Smelting, forging, and the quiet business of ammunition
origin_story: The foundry crews who reprocess scrap into cartridges, casings, and tools. They sell to anyone with trade goods and no questions, and their forges never go cold. In a world of shortages, they are the nearest thing to a mint.
key_beliefs: Steel remembers its shape
A loaded round is a vote
The forge has no politics

ideology: Debt, discipline, and the promise of redemption by labour
origin_story: A unit formed from those convicted or condemned after the exchange, worked in the quarries and the trench works under armed supervision. The battalion believes the sentence can be served, the debt paid, the name cleaned. The office believes the same, for different reasons.
key_beliefs: The debt can be worked off
Discipline is the only mercy
Names can be reclaimed

ideology: Local defence, neighbourhood watch, no ranks
origin_story: Community militias that formed to hold ground after the garrison pulled back: farmers with rifles, mechanics with shotguns. They are neighbours first and soldiers second, and they fight for the street they live on, not for a flag.
key_beliefs: The street is the unit
Defend, do not march
Every neighbour is a brother

ideology: Logistics, depots, and the paperwork of survival
origin_story: The quartermaster network that keeps depots stocked and convoys rolling. They are not fighters; they are accountants with rifles, and they know exactly what everyone owes, stores, and wastes.
key_beliefs: Count everything twice
A depot is a fortress
Paperwork is logistics

ideology: Plunder, movement, and the logic of the ambush
origin_story: Bands that live off the road and the raid, striking convoys and caches and vanishing into the ruins. They are not a state and not a tribe; they are a condition the wasteland produces, like rust or radiation.
key_beliefs: Take what moves
The road belongs to the ambush
Mercy is a loaded word
